# <span id="page-181-0"></span>*2004 Spatial Surveys*

During ASRAMP 2004, 50 shallow-water CTD casts were conducted in nearshore waters around Ofu and Olosega over the periods February 6–8 and 13 (Fig. 4.4.1d).

--- SENTENCE 2289 ---
Data from these vertical profiles showed spatial patterns that are notably different from the 2002 surveys, with relatively well-mixed water columns around both islands (Fig. 4.4.1e).

--- SENTENCE 2290 ---
The ranges of temperature and salinity variations around the islands over the depth profiles (0–30 m) were < 0.8°C and 35–35.5 psu, respectively.

--- SENTENCE 2291 ---
Salinity and density were lowest and beam transmission was highest (low turbidity) on the eastern side of Olosega (F–G).

--- SENTENCE 2292 ---
Since the water in the area was much fresher in the upper part of the water column (0–10 m) than near the bottom (20–30 m), the likely cause of this signal may have been runoff from the east side of Olosega.

--- SENTENCE 2293 ---
The low density, low salinity surface lens that this created appeared to subsequently get mechanically mixed vertically deeper into the water column by trade winds and wave action.

--- SENTENCE 2294 ---
The west side of Ofu in the northwest and southwest regions (K–B) was characterized by warm, fresh, turbid, and less dense surface waters (0–10 m) and cooler, more saline, and more dense bottom waters (20–30 m).

--- SENTENCE 2295 ---
Finally, an area of relatively well-mixed cool water (~ 29.2°C) extending from the surface to the bottom was observed in the south central region (I–J), just west of Asaga Strait, the shallow channel between the two islands.

# **4.4.2 Temporal Comparison—Hydrographic Data**

During each of the ASRAMP survey periods in 2002, 2004 and 2006, the nearshore CTD and water quality data exhibited noteworthy spatial heterogeneity, though actual ranges of most properties were relatively small.

--- SENTENCE 2334 ---
Temperature variations were small between sample periods.

--- SENTENCE 2335 ---
Salinity showed minimal variability between sample periods; however, salinity values were considerably lower during 2006.

--- SENTENCE 2336 ---
Density observations tended to parallel salinity more so than temperature, which is typically the dominant constituent when computing density.

--- SENTENCE 2337 ---
Turbidity measurements, when comparing 2004 and 2006, were extremely low at select locations in the latter survey period; the reason is unknown without additional observations.

--- SENTENCE 2338 ---

# *2006 Spatial Surveys*

Coral health and disease REA surveys covered a total survey area of 4800 m2 around Ofu and Olosega during ASRAMP 2006.

--- SENTENCE 2475 ---
A total of 22 cases of coral disease and predation were detected, translating to an estimated overall mean prevalence of 0.05% (SE 0.03; Figs.

--- SENTENCE 2476 ---
Around Ofu and Olosega, bleaching and growth anomalies were the only two afflictions observed to affect corals within the 10–15 m depth contours.

--- SENTENCE 2477 ---
Of the 12 sites surveyed, coral diseases were observed at 50%; the northeast, northwest, southeast, and southwest regions exhibited the majority of cases.

--- SENTENCE 2478 ---
Overall, the most common affliction encountered was bleaching, which affected corals in the genera *Platygyra*, *Leptoria*, *Montipora*, and *Porites*.

--- SENTENCE 2479 ---
Prevalence of bleaching did not exceed 0.16%, and bleaching was generally mild and focal within colonies.

--- SENTENCE 2480 ---
Prevalence of skeletal growth anomalies amounted to 0.16% at site OLO-01, on the east coast of Olosega, where all cases were detected.

--- SENTENCE 2481 ---
Interestingly, all cases of growth anomalies occurred only on *Acropora abrotanoides*.

--- SENTENCE 2482 ---
Finally, signs of *Acanthaster* and *Drupella* predation were observed at sites OLO-04 and OLO-06, where prevalence values amounted to 0.01 and 0.14%, respectively.

# **4.5.3 Temporal Comparison—Coral and Coral Disease**

The distribution of high scleractinian coral cover observed during towed-diver benthic surveys around Ofu and Olosega over the three ASRAMP cruises was sporadic, which is likely a result of natural variation and differing towed-diver depths between survey years.

--- SENTENCE 2490 ---
The overall means of towed-diver coral cover around Ofu and Olosega were between 14% and 20% (Fig. 4.5.3a).

--- SENTENCE 2491 ---
However, locations around the two islands show elevated coral cover levels across the three survey years.

--- SENTENCE 2492 ---
The northeast and southeast regions of Olosega showed consistent high coral cover, especially around the east and west sides of Maga Point, with mean values of 43.3%, 43.6%, and 42.3% in 2002, 2004, and 2006, respectively.

--- SENTENCE 2493 ---
High coral cover was also recorded along the southern coast of Nu`utele Island and along Nu`usilaelae Island in 2002 and 2006 (mean: 31% and 27%, respectively).

--- SENTENCE 2494 ---
Shallower towed-diver tracks roughly corresponded with areas of elevated coral cover over all years.

--- SENTENCE 2495 ---
Mean island-wide live scleractinian coral percent cover around Ofu and Olosega during ASRAMP 2004 and 2006 REA surveys were 25.3% (SE 6.3) and 29.0% (SE 4.8), respectively (Fig. 4.5.3a).

--- SENTENCE 2496 ---
Although these values are similar, it is important to note the methods to estimate coral percent cover were different in 2004 (visual estimates) and 2006 (line point intercept technique).

--- SENTENCE 2497 ---

--- SENTENCE 2518 ---
# <span id="page-209-0"></span>**4.6 Algae**

It is important to note when considering these results that turf algae, crustose coralline red algae, branched non-geniculate coralline red algae, and cyanophytes (blue-green algae) all need to be analyzed microscopically for proper taxonomic identification and, therefore, must be lumped into functional group categories in the field.

--- SENTENCE 2519 ---
Of these functional groups, turf algae are the most diverse with the possibility of up to 100 species occurring in a 10 cm2 area.

--- SENTENCE 2520 ---
As well, macroalgae are large, fleshy, sometimes calcified entities that may be identifiable to genus or species in the field, but often require microscopic analysis to confirm taxonomic identities.

--- SENTENCE 2521 ---

#### <span id="page-214-0"></span>**4.6.2 Coralline Algal Disease Surveys**

# *2006 Spatial Surveys*

Coralline algal diseases were abundant at Ofu and Olosega with a total of 278 cases enumerated (Figs. 4.6.2a and 4.6.2b).

--- SENTENCE 2577 ---
Coralline algal disease was detected at all sites, except for OFU-03, on the south-facing shore.

--- SENTENCE 2578 ---
More than 75% of all cases detected were found at sites OFU-01, -04, and -08 in the central north, central south, and northwest regions.

--- SENTENCE 2579 ---
Two types of coralline afflictions were detected: coralline lethal orange disease (CLOD) and an unidentified coralline discoloration.

--- SENTENCE 2580 ---
CLOD was common and abundant, accounting for greater than 96% of all coralline algal disease cases.

# **4.6.3 Temporal Comparison—Algae**

Temporal comparisons of both REA algal data and towed-diver survey data are shown in Figures 4.6.3a and 4.6.3b, respectively.

--- SENTENCE 2586 ---
A greater sampling density around Ofu and Olosega during ASRAMP 2006 allowed for a more complete picture of algal populations.

--- SENTENCE 2587 ---
Populations of the calcified, geniculate red algal genera *Amphiroa/Jania* were more evenly distributed and of greater abundance around the two islands than was indicated during the ASRAMP 2004 sampling period.

--- SENTENCE 2588 ---
Cyanophytes also exhibited a much higher and more evenly distributed pattern around the islands than was previously discerned.

--- SENTENCE 2589 ---
Distributional patterns of the calcified, sand-producing green alga, *Halimeda*, remained similar between survey periods.

--- SENTENCE 2590 ---
As in 2004, lowest algal diversity and abundance occurred off the populated coast of Ofu Village.

--- SENTENCE 2591 ---
As also noted for Ta`u (Section 5.6), a dramatic difference between the number of algal genera and their abundance was reported around Ofu and Olosega between the 2004 and 2006 sampling periods.

--- SENTENCE 2592 ---
In 2004, Ofu and Olosega did not exhibit much diversity of macroalgal genera, but by 2006 they contained macroalgal populations almost twice as diverse as seen in 2004.

--- SENTENCE 2593 ---
Although Tropical Cyclone Heta did not pass directly over the Manu`a Islands, it is

hypothesized that severe wave energy generated from the storm scoured benthic communities shortly before 2004 surveys were conducted, shredding algal communities and making the islands appear to have low algal diversity.

--- SENTENCE 2594 ---
By 2006, observations of the algal communities suggest they may have fully recovered.

# **4.8.2 Temporal Comparison—Reef Fish**

The three ASRAMP survey periods in 2002, 2004, and 2006 showed no clear geographic patterns of total fish biomass around Ofu and Olosega.

--- SENTENCE 2720 ---
The majority of the biomass was herbivorous surgeonfish and parrotfish.

--- SENTENCE 2721 ---
Total fish biomass around these islands was slightly above 1 tons ha-1 in 2002 and 2004 but appears to have decreased to 0.54 tons ha-1 in 2006 (Fig. 4.8.2a).

--- SENTENCE 2722 ---
Overall, total fish biomass is around 1.0 tons ha-1 (SE 0.3) for Ofu and Olosega.

#### **4.9 Island Summary and Integration**

Ofu and Olosega are extremely steep, quickly eroding volcanic islands in the Manu`a Island group that are located in an area that remains geologically dynamic and active.

--- SENTENCE 2733 ---
Bathymetric and backscatter data from multibeam surveys (Figs. 4.3.1a and 4.3.1b) around the islands revealed the presence of a narrow (~ 1 km) insular shelf, with banks extending off the northwestern, northeastern, and southeastern sides up to 2 km offshore.

--- SENTENCE 2734 ---
The shelf and banks were generally composed of mostly hard substrate extending seaward from the reef crest.

--- SENTENCE 2735 ---
Sand fields were also located at the base of the forereef slope off the watershed drainage areas on the north sides of both islands visible within the backscatter imagery (Fig. 4.3.1b), which corresponded with shallower towed-diver observations that found high levels of sand cover in the central north and northwest regions (Fig.

--- SENTENCE 2736 ---
Towed-diver observations in the north also noted elevated sand cover and habitat complexity within/east of the Asaga Strait separating Ofu and Olosega, suggesting sand channel(s) in rugose habitat (Figs.

--- SENTENCE 2737 ---
Two broad sand channels were identified off the east side of Olosega that merged into a sand field at the base of the forereef slope in that location.

--- SENTENCE 2738 ---
Along the northeast windward coast of Olosega, towed-diver surveys also identified an area of moderate-high complexity corresponding with low/moderate sand cover that was immediately followed by an area of low complexity with a visible parallel change from low to high sand cover.

--- SENTENCE 2739 ---
In each of the ASRAMP survey periods in 2002, 2004, and 2006, the nearshore CTD and water quality observations exhibited spatial heterogeneity, though in many cases the ranges of the spatial changes were relatively small.

--- SENTENCE 2740 ---
Between survey periods, temperature and salinity variations were generally small.

--- SENTENCE 2741 ---
Despite the relatively small changes in physical properties, some spatial patterns around Ofu and Olosega were clear.

--- SENTENCE 2742 ---
A particularly cool episode, with temperatures reaching nearly 2°C below the SST climatology, was observed in austral winter 2002 before sharply rising 3°C to climatologically normal temperatures in late 2002.

--- SENTENCE 2743 ---
In situ temperature observations generally tracked satellite-derived temperature products rather closely, with one exception in early 2005, when in situ values were nearly 1.5°C above satellite SST.

--- SENTENCE 2744 ---
Salinity values island-wide were considerably lower during the 2006 surveys in comparison with previous years and may be attributed to aboveaverage rainfall (Fig. 3.4.3d).

--- SENTENCE 2745 ---
Density observations tended to parallel salinity more closely than temperature, which is typically the dominant constituent when computing density.

--- SENTENCE 2746 ---
Turbidity levels, when comparing 2004 and 2006, were extremely high at select locations in the latter survey period (Fig. 4.4.1i), most likely a result of the exceptional precipitation preceding the ASRAMP 2006 surveys.

--- SENTENCE 2747 ---
In general, the northern coastline, including the northwest, central north, and northeast regions was characterized by infrequent, long period swells from North Pacific boreal winter storms, while the southern coastline, including the southwest, central south, and southeast regions, was characterized by frequent short period (8–12 sec) waves (~ 2 m) from trade wind swells and less frequent, larger (~ 3 m), longer period (12–18 sec) swells generated by winter storms in the Southern Ocean (Fig. 3.4.3f).

--- SENTENCE 2748 ---
Aside from the large-scale east to west currents, no nearshore current data are available to resolve finer scale patterns.

--- SENTENCE 2749 ---
The forereef slope off the north side of Ofu in the central north region and the eastern portion of the northwest region was characterized during towed-diver benthic surveys as having very high habitat complexity, moderate levels of sand, hard substrate/pavement, and rubble, and moderate-to-low live coral cover (Figs. 4.3.2a, 4.3.2b, 4.3.2c, 4.3.2d, and 4.3.2e).

--- SENTENCE 2750 ---
Combined, these characteristics describe the high-relief spur-and-groove habitat of the area, reflecting the regions exposure to significant wave energy during austral summer months as long period ocean swells from the northwest sector (Fig.

--- SENTENCE 2751 ---
3.4.3f) impact the biogeography of these northern exposed reefs, despite the fact that these swells are generated by North Pacific winter storms located more than 5000 km away.

--- SENTENCE 2752 ---
Other results from the 2004 and 2006 surveys were likely influenced by the large-swell event generated by Tropical Cyclone Heta in January 2004.

--- SENTENCE 2753 ---
In 2004, the eastern side of Olosega displayed low salinity and density values, and high-beam transmission values (low turbidity), suggesting the presence of a freshwater lens during the sampling period in that region (Figs.

--- SENTENCE 2754 ---
The cause of this signal was likely rainfall and subsequent runoff from the many streams which line the east side of Olosega, which may have caused an influx of freshwater to the surface waters that mixed deeper into the water column through trade wind and wave action.

--- SENTENCE 2755 ---
In contrast, the western part of the island group showed localized variability, including the lowest measured beam transmission values (high turbidity) of the survey period.

--- SENTENCE 2756 ---
While the western side of Ofu also has a number of mapped streams, no evidence of a freshwater influx was observed in the 2004 nearshore CTD survey data.

--- SENTENCE 2757 ---
Conversely, in 2006, the eastern part of the island group showed much more local variability in these physical oceanographic parameters, including a region with some of the lowest measured beam transmission values (Figs.

--- SENTENCE 2758 ---
The area around the northern Asaga Strait was characterized by relatively high water temperature and beam transmission values, along with low salinity and density values.

--- SENTENCE 2759 ---
These characteristics suggest a freshwater feature at that location during the sampling period in 2006 because of rainwater runoff and the formation of a freshwater lens near the surface, or through some other mechanism that was undetected.

--- SENTENCE 2760 ---
In contrast, the western coastline displayed relatively cold, saline, and dense water, suggesting a possible upwelling feature in that region (Figs.

--- SENTENCE 2761 ---
The leeward sides of both Ofu and Olosega were observed to be more stratified than around most of the rest of the islands, likely indicating surface heating and lack of wave-induced vertical mixing.

--- SENTENCE 2762 ---
The southwestern shoreline of Olosega showed the highest total nitrogen (Ntot; Fig.

--- SENTENCE 2763 ---
4.4.1j) in the American Samoa Archipelago, possibly indicating a deep subsurface source.

--- SENTENCE 2764 ---
Sites near the northwest village of Ofu and the town of Olosega along the southern coast all showed higher Chlorophyll-a values than most of the other areas of the island group (Fig. 4.4.1j).

--- SENTENCE 2765 ---
Figure 4.3.2e shows estimates of live coral percent cover from towed-diver surveys integrated across the survey years and probably provides the most complete picture of live coral distribution patterns.

--- SENTENCE 2766 ---
The highest consistent live coral cover values were recorded along the east-facing, windward coast in the northeast and southeast regions of Olosega, which mirrored localized areas of moderate-to-high habitat complexity that bordered low-complexity sand channels (Figs.

--- SENTENCE 2767 ---
The east and west sides of Maga Point at the southern tip of Olosega in the southeast region also showed especially high live coral cover, with mean values of 43.3%, 43.6%, and 42.3% in 2002, 2004, and 2006, respectively (Figs.

--- SENTENCE 2768 ---
4.5.1b, 4.5.1e, and 4.5.1k).

--- SENTENCE 2769 ---
Additional high coral cover areas varied by year, and included areas of the central south and northwest regions (Figs. 4.5.1b, 4.5.1e, and 4.5.1k).

--- SENTENCE 2770 ---
Since towed-diver survey tracks varied between the survey years, Figure 4.3.2e also shows gradients of live coral cover in the inshore-offshore (shallow-deep) direction.

--- SENTENCE 2771 ---
In many areas, such as the east and west sides of Maga Point in the southeast region, higher live coral cover values were observed in the shallower inshore areas.

--- SENTENCE 2772 ---
In other areas, high live coral cover values were observed at intermediate or deeper depths further offshore.

--- SENTENCE 2773 ---
These observed patterns support the hypothesis that coral community structure is both spatially heterogeneous and depth-stratified around Ofu and Olosega.

--- SENTENCE 2774 ---
These patterns were likewise observed during TOAD optical surveys, where there were few colonies observed during offshore and relatively deep tows (Fig. 4.3.1c).

--- SENTENCE 2775 ---
On each of the three relatively shallow banks extending off corners of the two islands, coral communities were noted, specifically on the submerged banks in the southeast, northeast, and northwest regions.

--- SENTENCE 2776 ---
Interestingly, some of these communities occurred at depths greater than ~ 50 m, which indicates that coral stratification does not necessarily preclude the formation of deeper colonies.

--- SENTENCE 2777 ---
Though deeper coral communities are generally limited by penetration of sufficient light to support photosynthesis, their depth

provides some ecological benefits, such as significantly reduced exposure to damaging wave energy from surface gravity waves.

--- SENTENCE 2778 ---
Similarly, coral growth and depth stratification patterns noted during towed-diver and TOAD surveys were also mirrored in some of the REA surveys between years.

--- SENTENCE 2779 ---
For example, site OFU-02, located on the southwestern corner of Ofu in the southwest region, shows mixed results between years.

--- SENTENCE 2780 ---
In 2004, low coral cover, low coral density, and high diversity were recorded.

--- SENTENCE 2781 ---
In 2006, a survey at the presumed same site revealed a threefold increase in coral cover, a twofold increase in coral density, and a 20% reduction in the number of reported genera.

--- SENTENCE 2782 ---
A closer examination of dive metadata revealed that the 2004 survey of OFU-02 was completed in water depths ranging between ~ 5 and ~ 15 m, while the 2006 survey was completed in depths ranging between ~ 14 and 20 m. In this case, the higher coral cover and density were observed in the deeper depth range, possibly a reflection of the increased wave energy in the shallower habitat.

--- SENTENCE 2783 ---
A total of 34 coral genera were found around Ofu and Olosega.

--- SENTENCE 2784 ---
*Montipora* and *Goniastrea* were the most dominant genera in 2004 and 2006, with *Porites* and *Pocillopora* also appearing dominant in 2004 and 2006, respectively (Figs. 4.5.1g and 4.5.1m).

--- SENTENCE 2809 ---
There are a number of potential hypotheses for some of these observed trends.

--- SENTENCE 2810 ---
Larger, more stable coral communities at sites OLO-01 and OLO-05 in the northeast and central north regions may have higher coral cover, larger colonies, diminished species richness, and decreased colony densities as a result of protected cover from large swells generated by southern storms and/or other moderate-to-high levels of environmental disturbance (Fig. 3.4.3f).

--- SENTENCE 2811 ---
Though site OLO-01 on the east side of Olosega is exposed to prevailing trade wind swells, it is generally protected from the larger swell wave energy from both the south and northwest, which may help explain why that area has the highest live coral cover and largest coral size class distributions around Ofu and Olosega.

--- SENTENCE 2812 ---
Being exposed to persistent trade wind-driven ocean circulation, the reefs in that area are continually flushed and nourished, yet they are not exposed to the extreme and destructive wave events of other areas around these two islands.

--- SENTENCE 2813 ---
The vertical profiles of water properties for the shallow-water CTD surveys generally found the east end of Olosega to have a well-mixed water column, suggesting an increased likelihood of localized upwelling of nutrients (Figs. 4.4.1b and 4.4.1e).

--- SENTENCE 2814 ---
High coral densities of smaller colonies in portions of the central south and southwest regions might be congruent with higher levels of species richness, also suggesting an oceanographic link to wave energy.

--- SENTENCE 2815 ---
Sea surface temperature observations between February 2002 and February 2004 revealed no evidence of temperatures exceeding the bleaching threshold, and no large-scale bleaching was observed during ASRAMP 2002 or 2004 surveys.

#### <span id="page-238-0"></span>**Chapter 5 Ta`u Island**

# **5.1 Geopolitical Context**

Ta`u Island is the easternmost member of the Manu`a Island group, located ~ 150 km northeast of Tutuila Island and ~ 20 km east of Olosega Island.

--- SENTENCE 2846 ---
Ta`u, with a land area of 44 km2 , is an extremely steep volcanic island ringed by sea cliffs, some nearly 600 m high, with limited low altitude, level land areas.

--- SENTENCE 2847 ---
The seafloor surrounding Ta`u drops steeply, sometimes almost vertically, to abyssal.

--- SENTENCE 2848 ---
Collapse and landslides off the remnants of the southern caldera resulted in a south-facing embayment with a steep headwall that overlooks several flat benches, with the most prominent being the Liu Bench overlooking Papaloaloa Point (Fig. 5.1a).

--- SENTENCE 2849 ---
Between Olosega and Ta`u lies an unnamed submerged volcanic ridge and cone that was previously active in 1866 (Craig, 2002), and more recently mapped between 2004 and 2006.

--- SENTENCE 2850 ---
The broader area is still considered to be geologically active since the submerged volcanic cone of Vailulu`u Seamount is rapidly (in a geologic sense) forming approximately 50 km east of Ta`u.

Ta`u is divided into three counties: Faleasao County, Fiti`uta County, and Ta`u County.

--- SENTENCE 2851 ---
The population of Ta`u has mirrored similar trends reported at Ofu and Olosega Islands, with larger populations recorded in the mid-20th century that have seen a steady decline over the course of the last 60 years.

--- SENTENCE 2852 ---
Cyclones Tusi (1987), Ofa (1990), and Val (1991) resulted in

!

--- SENTENCE 2853 ---
** Watershed boundaries, streams, landmarks and villages for Ta`u.

--- SENTENCE 2854 ---
Also shown is the boundary for the National Park of American Samoa (NPAS).

--- SENTENCE 2855 ---
<span id="page-239-0"></span>approximately one-third of the population moving to Tutuila (Meehl, 1996).

--- SENTENCE 2856 ---
The current population of Ta`u was recently estimated at a total of 873 people (U.S. Census Bureau, 2000), with 135 people in Faleāsao County, 380 in Ta`u County, and 358 in Fiti`uta County.

--- SENTENCE 2857 ---
The residents of Ta`u rely primarily on subsistence farming, agroforestry, and fishing.

--- SENTENCE 2858 ---
There is a relatively low level of tourism to the island.

--- SENTENCE 2859 ---
The majority of the residential, agricultural, and commercial land remains in the north and west sides of the island, while the southern and eastern portions remain mostly under the jurisdiction of the NPAS.

--- SENTENCE 2860 ---
Several particular areas and landmarks of Ta`u are notable.

--- SENTENCE 2861 ---
A boat harbor is located in the northwestern corner of the island between Utumanu`a Point and Si`ulagi Point near the village of Faleāsao (Fig. 5.1a).

--- SENTENCE 2862 ---
The village of Ta`u is located to the south of Faleāsao, along a road that ends halfway down the western coastline.

--- SENTENCE 2863 ---
From Ta`u, the same road continues east of Faleāsao passing the airport runway, located near Fiti`uta Point and the village of Fiti`uta, and continues along the eastern coastline before ending near Tufu Point in the southeast.

--- SENTENCE 2864 ---
Finally, the NPAS begins halfway between Fiti`uta Point and Tufu Point, and continues along the southern coastline, ending near Si`ufa`alele Point in the southwest.

--- SENTENCE 2865 ---
# **5.2 Survey Effort**

A large amount of physical and biological data have been collected around Ta`u since 2002 as

!

--- SENTENCE 2866 ---
Locations of (Rapid Ecological Assessment

--- SENTENCE 2867 ---
[REA] and towed-diver surveys around Ta`u during ASRAMP 2002, 2004, and 2006.

--- SENTENCE 2868 ---
Four arbitrary geographic regions have been delineated to aid in discussion of spatial patterns.

--- SENTENCE 2869 ---
part of the Pacific Islands Fisheries Science Center (PIFSC)

--- SENTENCE 2870 ---
Coral Reef Ecosystem Division's (CRED's) American Samoa Reef Assessment and Monitoring Program (ASRAMP).

--- SENTENCE 2871 ---
The extent and timeframe of these survey efforts are discussed below.

--- SENTENCE 2872 ---

--- SENTENCE 2898 ---
<span id="page-242-0"></span>**5.3 Benthic Habitat Mapping and Characterization**

Benthic habitat mapping and characterization of the nearshore waters around Ta`u were conducted using acoustic multibeam sonar, underwater video and still imagery, and toweddiver survey observations between ~ 1 and ~ 250 m (and deeper).

--- SENTENCE 2899 ---
Acoustic multibeam sonar mapping provided bathymetric and backscatter data products for depths between ~ 20 and ~ 250 m. Optical validation and benthic characterization via underwater video, still imagery, and diver observations were performed using both shipboard towed cameras (i.e., TOAD) in depths between ~ 20 and ~ 80 m and towed-diver surveys in depths between ~ 1 and 30 m.

#### **5.3.1 Acoustic Mapping and Optical Validation**

Because Ta`u is a steep volcanic island with almost no offshore bank areas, depths of 350 m and greater were found less than 1 km offshore (Fig. 5.3.1a).

--- SENTENCE 2900 ---
A series of small, relatively shallow, seamount features were discovered ~ 2 km to the northwest of Utumanu`a Point on the northwestern corner of Ta`u.

--- SENTENCE 2901 ---
Some of these seamount summits are as shallow as 38 m.

The backscatter imagery acquired during the ASRAMP 2004 surveys was successfully used as a predictive guide for determining sites for the optical surveys conducted during ASRAMP

!

--- SENTENCE 2902 ---
** Multibeam bathymetry acquisition around Ta`u in depths between ~ 10 and ~ 350 m was completed in March 2004, from the R/V *Acoustic Habitat Investigator* (*AHI*).

--- SENTENCE 2903 ---
The island drops steeply from all sides and is connected to Olosega via a series of small seamounts along a submerged ridge tending toward the northwest.

!

--- SENTENCE 2904 ---
** Backscatter imagery was acquired in March 2004 during multibeam surveys around Ta`u from the R/V *AHI*.

--- SENTENCE 2906 ---
Darker shades represent high-intensity backscatter and likely indicate consolidated hard-bottom and coral substrates.

--- SENTENCE 2907 ---

--- SENTENCE 2908 ---
During TOAD camera surveys of these seamounts during ASRAMP 2006, video observations confirmed the presence of living corals.

--- SENTENCE 2909 ---

# <span id="page-245-0"></span>**5.3.2 Habitat Characterization**

Towed-diver benthic survey observations around Ta`u from ASRAMP 2002, 2004, and 2006 were concatenated into mean spatial distributions of benthic composition (see Chapter 2, Section 2.2.3: Optical Validation Surveys).

--- SENTENCE 2921 ---
These analyses for Ta`u are presented as mean distributions of habitat complexity (Fig. 5.3.2a) and percent cover of sand (Fig. 5.3.2b), hard substrate/pavement (Fig. 5.3.2c), rubble (Fig. 5.3.2d), and live coral (Fig. 5.3.2e).

--- SENTENCE 2922 ---
Since these habitat characterization maps represent different complementary components of the same habitat, it is useful to analyze them in relation to each other, the local watersheds, and exposure to prevailing oceanographic conditions.

--- SENTENCE 2923 ---
Habitat complexity was observed to vary significantly around Ta`u, with observations ranging from low to very high (Fig. 5.3.2a).

--- SENTENCE 2924 ---
Habitat complexity appeared high to very high in portions of the east, south, and north regions.

--- SENTENCE 2925 ---
High to very high habitat complexity was observed along an ~ 1 km stretch of the forereef slope in the east region, specifically the area near the midpoint between Tiafou Point at the northeast corner and Tufu Point at the southeast corner.

--- SENTENCE 2926 ---
In this particular area, towed divers have recorded observations of extremely large massive Porites coral heads, some exceeding 5-6 m in height and 14 m in diameter (Figs.

--- SENTENCE 2927 ---
** Mean benthic habitat complexity concatenated from towed-diver survey observations around Ta`u during ASRAMP 2002, 2004, and 2006.

--- SENTENCE 2928 ---
Habitat complexity was subjectively rated by divers over 5-min ensembles (~ 200 m × 10 m) on a 6-point scale representing low (1), medium-low (2), medium (3), mediumhigh (4), high (5), and very high (6) topographic complexity.

--- SENTENCE 2929 ---
Yellow colors indicate low habitat complexity, and dark green colors indicate high habitat complexity.

!

--- SENTENCE 2930 ---
** Mean percent cover of sand concatenated from towed-diver benthic survey observations around Ta`u during ASRAMP 2002, 2004, and 2006.

--- SENTENCE 2932 ---
Sand composition was subjectively rated by divers over 5-min ensembles (~ 200 m × 10 m) over a 1–100% scale.

--- SENTENCE 2933 ---
Light shades indicate high percent cover of sand, and dark shades indicate low percent cover of sand.

--- SENTENCE 2934 ---
An additional area of high complexity was noted along the south coast, specifically under the Liu Bench embayment and underneath the headwall surrounding Papaloaloa Point.

--- SENTENCE 2935 ---
In this area, divers observed a dramatic vertical rock wall descending as far as visibility allowed (~ 40 m).

--- SENTENCE 2936 ---
Few areas of high habitat complexity were also observed widely scattered in the north region.

--- SENTENCE 2937 ---
Areas of lower habitat complexity were recorded in a number of regions, specifically near Si`ufa`alele Point along the southwest corner of the island, in the vicinity of the village of Ta`u in the west region and in isolated, clearly defined areas in the north region.

--- SENTENCE 2938 ---

--- SENTENCE 2944 ---
Generally, the mean percent cover of coral rubble around Ta`u from towed-diver survey observations was consistently low, with typical values less than 5% (Fig. 5.3.2d).

--- SENTENCE 2945 ---
In a few areas, particularly along the forereef slope in the west region, there were stretches where observed values were closer to 25%.

--- SENTENCE 2946 ---

--- SENTENCE 2947 ---
The highest observed mean percent covers of live scleractinian coral were recorded in the east region between Tiafou Point and Tufu Point, with values ranging from 30% to 75%, and in the eastern portion of the south region near Ulufala Point, with similar high values (Fig. 5.3.2e).

--- SENTENCE 2948 ---

--- SENTENCE 3029 ---
The in situ nutrient data collected at Ta`u displayed the following ranges: chlorophyll-a (Chl-a), 0.26–0.69 µg L¹; phosphate (PO₄), 0.04–0.15 µM; silicate (SiO₂), 0.6–1.21 µM; and total nitrogen (N<sub>tot</sub> = NO₃ + NO₂), 0.23–0.64 µM. Water samples showed an increase in Chl-a concentrations near the harbor area, while most other nutrient concentrations showed increased values along the south shore of Ta`u (Fig. 5.4.1j).

--- SENTENCE 3030 ---
The south shore of Ta`u has the highest SiO₂ values in the American Samoa Archipelago.

--- SENTENCE 3031 ---
The south shore also exhibited a spike in PO₄ and NO₂ values.

--- SENTENCE 3032 ---
The vast majority of the population resides on the west coast, where nitrogen levels appeared elevated.

--- SENTENCE 3033 ---
There is also a small airport on the northeast corner of the island, although no increase in nutrients was observed in that area.

--- SENTENCE 3034 ---

**Figure 5.4.1j.

--- SENTENCE 3035 ---
** Interpolated Chl-a (top left), total nitrogen (top right), nitrate (middle left), nitrite (middle right), phosphate (bottom left) and silicate (bottom right) concentrations, at a 20-m depth derived from water samples collected in concert with shallow-water CTD casts around Ta`u during ASRAMP 2006, March 2–4.

#### **5.4.2 Temporal Comparison—Hydrographic Data**

During each of the ASRAMP survey periods in 2002, 2004, and 2006, the nearshore shallow-water CTD and water quality observations showed noteworthy spatial structure.

--- SENTENCE 3036 ---
Temperature, salinity, and density values each varied spatially during each survey periods, although observed patterns were not consistent between survey periods.

--- SENTENCE 3037 ---
Ta`u was similar to Ofu and Olosega in terms of nutrient results.

--- SENTENCE 3038 ---
Site-to-site variability within nutrient value results was slightly less than the variability seen around Tutuila.

--- SENTENCE 3039 ---
These results are a baseline for comparison with future nutrient datasets.

--- SENTENCE 3040 ---
It is important to note that substantial rainfall

<span id="page-261-0"></span>occurred during the survey period and that resulting terrestrial runoff affected results of the nutrient sampling.

#### **5.4.3 Time Series Observations**

A suite of moored instruments were deployed around Ta`u over the period between 2002 and 2006 to collect time series observations of key oceanographic properties influencing reef conditions (Fig. 5.4.3a).

--- SENTENCE 3041 ---
Deployment and retrieval dates of each instrument are detailed in Appendix II, Table II.iii.

--- SENTENCE 3042 ---
Figure 5.4.3b shows a time series of in situ and remotely sensed SST and modeled wave properties from January 2002 to April 2006.

--- SENTENCE 3043 ---
Pathfinder SST data from Ta`u showed predominantly seasonal variability with warmest temperatures (~ 30.0°C) observed during January–March and coolest temperatures (~ 27.5°C) in June–August (Fig.

--- SENTENCE 3044 ---
A particularly cool episode, with temperatures reaching nearly 1.5°C below SST climatology, was observed in austral winter 2002 before temperatures rose sharply to climatologically normal values in late 2002.

--- SENTENCE 3045 ---
In situ SST data were observed to be cooler and more variable when compared to Pathfinder SST temperature.

--- SENTENCE 3046 ---
Throughout most of the in situ record (July 2002–2004), moored SST values were observed to be 0°–3.5°C cooler than that observed via satellite and, for the most part, cooler when compared to the SST climatology.

--- SENTENCE 3047 ---
Telemetered in situ SST data from March 2004 to February 2005 correlated well with both Pathfinder SST and climatology.

--- SENTENCE 3106 ---
In 2004, the towed-diver methodology reported an estimate for percent live coral cover and stressed (pale/white) coral cover separately for each 5-min observation segment.

--- SENTENCE 3107 ---
To standardize the presentation of towed-diver benthic cover data between 2002 and 2004, live coral and stressed coral values from 2004 were summed to produce the total live coral category and then stressed coral was calculated as the percentage of live coral that was estimated as stressed.

--- SENTENCE 3108 ---
This may partially explain the high coral stress values reported for most areas where low coral cover was reported.

# <span id="page-278-0"></span>**5.5.2 Coral Disease Surveys**

# *2006 Spatial Surveys*

Coral health and disease REA surveys were conducted at nine sites around Ta`u during ASRAMP 2006 and covered a total survey area of 3850 m2 .

--- SENTENCE 3187 ---
Within this area, a total of 56 cases of coral disease, predation, and other types of lesions were enumerated.

--- SENTENCE 3188 ---
Of the nine sites surveyed, eight (89%) contained disease (Fig. 5.5.2a).

--- SENTENCE 3189 ---
Figure 5.5.2b illustrates the variation in prevalence of disease and predation among sites.

--- SENTENCE 3190 ---
Overall mean prevalence was 0.10% (SE 0.03).

--- SENTENCE 3191 ---
REA sites TAU-11 in the northwest corner and TAU-07 in the east region exhibited the greatest prevalence (0.27% and 0.29%, respectively; Fig. 5.5.2b).

--- SENTENCE 3192 ---
Skeletal growth anomaly was the most prevalent coral disease; 22 cases were detected, and within this disease category the scleractinian genera *Astreopora* and *Montipora* exhibited 50% of the documented cases.

--- SENTENCE 3193 ---
At site TAU-11, on the northwest corner, 50% of island-wide cases were detected.

--- SENTENCE 3194 ---
Bleaching was also detected at Ta`u, although with low prevalence (0.03%).

--- SENTENCE 3195 ---
Similarly to the other islands in the archipelago, bleaching was mild and focal.

--- SENTENCE 3196 ---
Scleractinian genera exhibiting bleaching included: *Montipora*, *Porites*, *Pocillopora*, and *Montastrea*.

--- SENTENCE 3197 ---
Other coral diseases observed at the survey sites included four cases of hyperpigmentation (dark spots) on *Astreopora*, *Pavona varians*, *Montipora*, and *Coscinaraea* (Fig. 5.5.2b).

!

#### **5.5.3 Temporal Comparison—Coral and Coral Disease**

High live scleractinian coral cover was consistently reported by towed-diver observers for surveys completed in 2002, 2004, and 2006 (Fig.

--- SENTENCE 3205 ---
5.5.3a), specifically along the east region windward coastline, beginning at Tiafou Point and heading south (42%, 38%, and 33%).

--- SENTENCE 3206 ---
Area surveyed along the south shore also recorded high coral cover in 2004 and 2006.

--- SENTENCE 3207 ---
Variations between years may be because of natural variation, changes in data collection protocol, trackline spacing (i.e., variation between towed-diver survey tracks between years), and observer variability resulting from changes in scientific personnel.

--- SENTENCE 3208 ---
Average percent live coral cover from 2004 REA surveys (24.3%, all nine sites) compared favorably with 2006 REA surveys (29.4%, same nine sites; Fig.

--- SENTENCE 3209 ---
When site TAU-10 is removed from the analysis (as transect lines were laid over substantially different substrate in each year), the cover estimates for both years become even more congruent (27.3% in 2004 vs. 30.5% in 2006).

--- SENTENCE 3210 ---
When comparing the estimates between years from site TAU-11, there are substantial differences (25% in 2004 vs. 54% in 2006).

--- SENTENCE 3211 ---
Visual estimates were used in 2004 to report coral cover whereas the line point intercept technique was used in 2006, and visual estimates can vary from those derived from the line point intercept technique even when made concurrently.

--- SENTENCE 3212 ---
CRED's coral survey methods have evolved over time; ideally, there should be two observers conducting coral surveys and the surveys should include quantitative population parameters and coral disease observations.

--- SENTENCE 3213 ---
This will allow for improved sitespecific comparisons to be made to surveys conducted in the future.

--- SENTENCE 3222 ---

--- SENTENCE 3223 ---
Again, it is hoped that personnel allocations and survey protocols will be the same in future years so that improved comparisons can be made.

#### **5.6 Algae**

#### **5.6.1 Algal Surveys**

# *2002 Spatial Surveys*

It is important to note when considering these results that turf algae, crustose coralline red algae, branched non-geniculate coralline red algae, and cyanophytes (blue-green algae) all need to be analyzed microscopically for proper taxonomic identification, and therefore, must be lumped into functional group categories in the field.

--- SENTENCE 3236 ---
Of these functional groups, turf algae are the most diverse with the possibility of up to 100 species occurring in a 10 cm2 area.

--- SENTENCE 3237 ---
As well, macroalgae are large, fleshy, sometimes calcified entities that may be identifiable to genus or species in the field but often require microscopic analysis to confirm taxonomic identities.

!

<span id="page-283-0"></span>Ten towed-diver surveys around Ta`u during ASRAMP 2002 found that combined fleshy macroalgal and crustose coralline red algal cover was 49.8%.

--- SENTENCE 3241 ---
The percent cover of crustose coralline red algae was relatively higher than fleshy macroalgae around Ta`u, with each functional group covering 34.9% (SE 1.3) and 14.9% (SE 1.2) of the benthic substrate, respectively (Fig. 5.6.1a).

--- SENTENCE 3242 ---
Crustose coralline red algal cover abundance was lowest along the northwestern corner of the island, while fleshy macroalgal cover abundance was among the highest.

--- SENTENCE 3243 ---
Qualitative REA algal surveys were conducted in 2002 around Ta`u, and six bags of algal voucher specimens were collected.

--- SENTENCE 3244 ---
These surveys provided baseline data used to design and scale the future methodology of algal REA surveys.

--- SENTENCE 3246 ---
Fleshy macroalgae were relatively uniform along the forereefs of Ta`u except for one towed-diver benthic survey near Siulagi Point in the north region, where percent cover averaged 58%.

--- SENTENCE 3248 ---

--- SENTENCE 3249 ---

# *2006 Spatial Surveys*

Fifteen towed-diver surveys around Ta`u during ASRAMP 2006 reported an average algal substrate cover of 37%.

--- SENTENCE 3271 ---
The percent cover of crustose coralline red algae was relatively higher than fleshy macroalgae around Ta`u, with each functional group covering 27.8% (SE 1.3) and 9.1% (SE 0.5) of the benthic substrate, respectively (Fig. 5.6.1e).

--- SENTENCE 3272 ---
Crustose coralline red algae were most abundant during tows along the east coast of the island, from Tiafou Point to Tufu Point, covering up to 50% of the benthic habitat.

--- SENTENCE 3273 ---
Quantitative algal surveys were conducted at eight of the same nine sites around Ta`u as were monitored in 2004 (site TAU-08 was not resurveyed; Fig. 5.6.1f).

--- SENTENCE 3274 ---
A total of 24 macroalgal genera (9 green, 13 red, and 2 brown) and 3 additional algal functional groups (turf algae, crustose coralline red algae, and cyanophytes) were observed in the field.

--- SENTENCE 3275 ---
Diversity of large, easily observed macroalgal genera (some of which contain multiple species) at each site ranged from 8 to 18, although once laboratory-based taxonomic identification of all algal species (including turf algae, epiphytes, and crustose coralline red algae) from each site is completed, algal diversity for each site will be much higher.

--- SENTENCE 3276 ---
Sites TAU-05 and TAU-09 in the north and west regions, respectively, exhibited the highest macroalgal generic diversity with 18 and 15 genera recorded, respectively.

--- SENTENCE 3277 ---
Divers recorded 8–9 genera at most other sites.

#### **5.6.3 Temporal Comparison—Algae**

A dramatic difference between the number of algal genera and their abundance was reported at Ta`u between the 2004 and 2006 sampling periods.

--- SENTENCE 3297 ---
In 2004, Ta`u exhibited the most meager algal community of all islands in American Samoa, but by 2006 it contained the most diverse and healthy algal community observed.

--- SENTENCE 3298 ---
Although Hurricane Heta did not pass over the Manu`a Island group, possibly severe wave energy generated from the storm in 2004 scoured benthic communities around Ta`u shortly before 2004 surveys were conducted, shredding algal communities and making the island appear to have low algal diversity.

--- SENTENCE 3299 ---
** Relative abundance of coralline algal disease around Ta`u during ASRAMP 2006.

--- SENTENCE 3300 ---
CLOD: coralline lethal orange disease; CFD: coralline fungal disease; and Other: undetermined coralline discolorations.

2006, the algal communities had fully recovered.

--- SENTENCE 3303 ---
Almost twice the number of genera was recorded in 2006 compared to 2004, and abundances of macroalgae in photoquadrats increased from < 25% to almost 100% at most sites (Fig. 5.6.3a).

--- SENTENCE 3304 ---
Macroalgal diversity, as determined through field observations of the relative abundance of macroalgae, was exceptionally higher along the northern shore of the island in 2006 as compared to 2004.

--- SENTENCE 3305 ---
As at Tutuila, a major difference between the 2004 and 2006 sampling periods was the presence of the red algal genera, *Amphiroa*/*Jania*, which were not recorded in 2004, but were extremely prevalent at almost every site in 2006.

--- SENTENCE 3306 ---
Populations of the green algae *Halimeda* and *Dictyosphaeria* remained relatively constant in both years, although *Dictyosphaeria* was very abundant at TAU-04 in 2006, whereas it was completely lacking in 2004.

#### <span id="page-303-0"></span>**5.9 Island Summary and Integration**

Ta`u is a small, steeply sloped island in the Manu`a Island chain.

--- SENTENCE 3424 ---
Bathymetric data from multibeam surveys around Ta`u reveal the presence of a narrow (< 1 km) shelf that is wider along the north and west sides of the island (Fig.

--- SENTENCE 3425 ---
A series of small seamounts are ~ 2 km northwest of Ta`u, along an east-west tending ridge, with depths as shallow as 38 m. The upper portions of this ridge of small, shallow seamounts were probably exposed during periods of lower sea level.

--- SENTENCE 3426 ---
Similarity between biota around neighboring islands probably derives from their spatial proximity which allows for substantial contemporary gene flow.

--- SENTENCE 3427 ---
Moreover, mapping efforts indicate a relatively shallow bridge between the islands that was likely historically exposed during lower stands of sea level, which may have provided stepping stones for colonization by taxa with short larval lifespans.

--- SENTENCE 3428 ---
TOAD optical validation surveys confirmed that these northwestern seamounts are colonized by coral communities (Fig. 5.3.1c).

--- SENTENCE 3429 ---
The benthic composition surrounding Ta`u was highly variable (Figs. 5.3.2a, 5.3.2b, 5.3.2c, 5.3.2d, and 5.3.2e).

--- SENTENCE 3430 ---
However, spatial and temporal patterns of the distributions of habitat types are apparent within the data.

--- SENTENCE 3431 ---
Low benthic topographical complexity was roughly correlated to the spatial distribution of sand (Fig. 5.3.2a).

--- SENTENCE 3432 ---
The south region, over the three survey periods, had consistently high benthic complexity, especially around Papaloaloa Point and the shoreline adjacent to the Liu Bench.

--- SENTENCE 3433 ---
High benthic complexity also was seen on the northern shore, but in smaller, more isolated areas.

--- SENTENCE 3434 ---
Because of the steeply sloped nature of Ta`u, terrestrial watersheds and existing drainages modify the marine benthic habitat (Fig. 5.1a).

--- SENTENCE 3435 ---
This is evident from concatenated toweddiver benthic habitat maps (Fig.

--- SENTENCE 3436 ---
5.3.2b) and multibeam backscatter maps (Fig. 5.3.1b).

--- SENTENCE 3437 ---
Sand and/or soft-bottom distribution on particularly the north shore benthos is directly correlated to terrestrial watersheds.

--- SENTENCE 3438 ---
There are also a few sand fields at the base of the forereef slope, especially off the western side of the island (Fig. 5.3.1b).

--- SENTENCE 3439 ---
While on a larger scale, physical oceanographic properties appeared to be somewhat homogeneous, distinct spatial patterns of all measured parameters were observed around Ta`u at smaller scales.

--- SENTENCE 3440 ---
There is believed to be a large-scale east-to-west current in the vicinity of Ta`u; however, no nearshore current data are available to resolve finer-scale patterns.

--- SENTENCE 3441 ---
Because of the steeply sloped nature of the island (Fig. 5.3.1a), the coral reef communities around Ta`u may be more exposed to wave energy than those at some of the other islands in American Samoa, such as Tutuila, which has a broad submerged bank that rises to depths as shallow as 20 m and extends several kilometers offshore.

--- SENTENCE 3442 ---
The north and west sides of Ta`u are exposed to infrequent, long-period swells from North Pacific boreal winter storms during the austral summer (Fig. 5.4.3b).

--- SENTENCE 3443 ---
The east and south sides of the island predominantly experience frequent short period (8–12 sec) waves (~ 2 m) from trade wind swell; they are also exposed to less frequent, larger (~ 3 m), longer period (12–18 sec) swells generated by winter storms in the Southern Ocean (Appendix II, Figure II.

--- SENTENCE 3444 ---
A large swell event from tropical cyclone Heta in January 2004 (Fig. 5.4.3b) appears to have had at least some impact on all sides of the island.

--- SENTENCE 3445 ---
During each of the ASRAMP survey periods in 2002, 2004, and 2006, the nearshore shallowwater CTD and water quality observations exhibited spatial heteorgeneity, although in many cases the magnitudes of the spatial changes were relatively modest (Figs.

--- SENTENCE 3446 ---
5.4.1b, 5.4.1e, and 5.4.1h).

--- SENTENCE 3447 ---
Waters in the east region were generally found to be well-mixed in the upper ~ 20 m of the water column, likely because of the influence of southeasterly trade winds.

--- SENTENCE 3448 ---
Interestingly, during mostly light-to-moderate winds for the survey periods, waters on the east side were generally stratified below ~ 20 m. The west region of the island was generally observed to have increased stratification in the upper water column, with the northern and southern sides falling in between.

--- SENTENCE 3449 ---
Water turbidity was highest along the central north region of Ta`u (Figs.

--- SENTENCE 3450 ---
5.4.1c, 5.4.1f, and 5.4.1i).

--- SENTENCE 3451 ---
Interpretation of salinity values from CTD data indicates there are likely point sources of fresh, cool water on the north side, probably from watersheds or subsurface springs.

--- SENTENCE 3452 ---
This would additionally account for the increase in turbidity values on the north side, as sediment input from terrigenous sources is often associated with freshwater outflows.

--- SENTENCE 3453 ---
Increases in turbidity could also be explained by austral summer swell from the northwest that could be stirring up benthic sediments.

--- SENTENCE 3454 ---
In situ SST values (July 2002–February 2004) were observed to be 0°–3.5°C cooler than those observed via satellite and, for the most part, cooler when compared to the SST climatology (Fig. 5.4.3b).

--- SENTENCE 3455 ---
Nutrient concentrations show increased values along the south shore of Ta`u, and elevated nitrogen levels were found on the west side (Fig. 5.4.1j).

--- SENTENCE 3456 ---
Water samples indicated an increase in Chl-a concentrations near the harbor area on the northwestern side of the island.

--- SENTENCE 3457 ---
In both 2004 and 2006, this area was observed to have elevated turbidity and low salinity, which may be indicative of a point source of sediment and freshwater input.

--- SENTENCE 3458 ---
A total of 32 coral genera have been observed around Ta`u, with higher diversity in the south region, and *Montipora*, *Astreopora*, *Favia*, and *Porites* being the most common.

--- SENTENCE 3459 ---
Approximately 64% of the coral colonies measured in 2004 (Fig. 5.5.1i), and 79% of them in 2006 (Fig. 5.5.1o), were relatively small (< 20 cm maximum diameter).

--- SENTENCE 3460 ---
The high percentages of small colonies may reflect periodic disturbances from large wave events.

--- SENTENCE 3461 ---
In contrast to most areas, abundant large colonies have been found at some sites on the northwestern and northern sides of the island, which are hypothesized to be have been somewhat more sheltered than other areas from large but infrequent Southern Ocean swell and tropical cyclones.

--- SENTENCE 3462 ---
That said, towed-diver benthic surveys along the central portion of the east region have observed, without quantification, areas with large *Porites* colonies.

--- SENTENCE 3463 ---
Massive *Porites* colonies were also observed in the west, and are believed to be among the largest known (~ 6 m in height and ~ 14 m in diameter), and possibly the oldest observed coral colonies in the world.

--- SENTENCE 3464 ---
Toweddiver benthic surveys also found a region in the southern portion of the west region that had similar, but slightly smaller, coral skeletons.

--- SENTENCE 3465 ---
Although the coral communities appear to mostly be healthy, 88% of REA sites on Ta`u were observed to contain minor amounts (< 0.3%) of diseased coral, mainly growth anomalies and bleaching (Figs.

--- SENTENCE 3466 ---
SST profiles between February 2002 and February 2004 reveal a short spike above the coral bleaching threshold in March 2002 (Fig. 5.4.3b).

--- SENTENCE 3467 ---
However, this spike was not of sufficient duration to be expected to trigger bleaching, and no substantial coral bleaching was observed during 2002 or 2004 surveys.

--- SENTENCE 3468 ---
Figure 5.3.2e shows towed-diver survey estimates of live scleractinian coral cover integrated between years and probably provides the most complete picture of higher coral cover areas.

--- SENTENCE 3469 ---
It indicates higher percent cover to the southeast and lower percent cover to the northwest.

--- SENTENCE 3470 ---
All four corners of the island have relatively low coral percent cover in nearshore waters, possibly a result of wave energy refracting and concentrating onto these areas during high wave events.

--- SENTENCE 3471 ---
Generally higher coral percent cover to the southeast may possibly reflect increased circulation, flushing, and mixing in response to increased exposure to persistent southeastern trade winds.

--- SENTENCE 3472 ---
Interestingly, these findings are similar to those on the east side of Olosega.

--- SENTENCE 3473 ---
Towed-diver surveys, most notably in 2006, suggested that high live coral cover and increased topographical complexity are tightly coupled (Fig. 5.5.1k).

--- SENTENCE 3474 ---
High coral cover recorded by towed-diver surveys was variably distributed around Ta`u and showed temporally consistent hotspots on the eastern and south coasts.

--- SENTENCE 3475 ---
The towed-diver and REA survey mean percent coral cover for all years was found to be approximately 25% for nearshore waters (Fig.

--- SENTENCE 3476 ---
Island-wide percentages of coral cover steadily declined between 2002 and 2006 in the towed-diver survey observations, while REA results showed an increase between 2004 and 2006.

--- SENTENCE 3477 ---
Towed-diver survey estimates of the percentage of stressed coral declined between 2004 and 2006 from ~ 6% to 2% (Figs.

--- SENTENCE 3478 ---
Locations around the island showing the highest coral cover varied between years, and to some degree results also varied by method.

--- SENTENCE 3479 ---
It is likely that the variations in results among different years (2002, 2004, and 2006) and survey methods (towed-diver surveys, visual estimates, and line point intercept) reflect differences in survey locations, changes in data collection protocols from year to year, and heterogeneity of coral distribution more than they do changes in coral community structure over time.

--- SENTENCE 3480 ---
Corals were mostly absent in the TOAD optical imagery from deeper (~ 30–80 m) areas.

--- SENTENCE 3481 ---
However, a coral community was found off the southeastern corner of the island.

--- SENTENCE 3482 ---
An additional luxuriant coral reef was observed over the summit of a shallow seamount 2 km northwest of Ta`u (Fig. 5.3.1c).

--- SENTENCE 3483 ---
It is important to include the extremely large and ancient communities of *Porites* sp. corals found on the east and west sides of the island (Figs.

--- SENTENCE 3484 ---
5.3.2f and 5.3.2g) when characterizing the coral communities of Ta`u.

--- SENTENCE 3485 ---
In the more protected southern portion of the west region, the colonies were mostly dead and decaying; however, these ancient and massive corals are thought to be between 500 and 1000 years old and may be among the oldest known living coral colonies found in the world.

--- SENTENCE 3486 ---
At the request of Governor Tulafono of American Samoa, CRED scientists provided images, video, and background information about these unique coral colonies for his presentation at the United States Coral Reef Task Force meeting in May 2006.

--- SENTENCE 3487 ---
At the time of publication, the American Samoa government is considering designation of this area as a Marine Protected Area.

--- SENTENCE 3488 ---
These massive and ancient coral colonies, some living and some dead, are unique and deserve special attention as objects of study to advance the conservation and management of coral reef ecosystems in American Samoa and elsewhere.

--- SENTENCE 3489 ---
Combined, they contain within their cores a unique history of climate and ecological impacts of climate change over the past 500–1000 years.

--- SENTENCE 3490 ---
Important questions concerning why the ancient corals have continued to thrive on the both the east and west sides of Ta`u, while their companion colonies on the west side have not, may improve our understanding of the ecological impacts of climate change

and therefore provide guidance on how to better manage and conserve coral reefs during upcoming climate changes.

--- SENTENCE 3491 ---
Turf algae and crustose coralline red algae were the dominant benthic organisms at most nearshore areas around Ta`u and were usually fairly uniformly distributed around the island with a few exceptions (Figs.

--- SENTENCE 3492 ---
5.6.1a, 5.6.1b, and 5.6.1e).

--- SENTENCE 3493 ---
The lowest cover of crustose coralline algae and the highest cover and diversity of macroalgae were found off the northwestern corner of the island.

--- SENTENCE 3494 ---
We hypothesize that the high concentration of macroalgae may be a result of the high influx of fresh water and terrestrial sediments mentioned previously and possibly terrestrial nutrients.

--- SENTENCE 3495 ---
Macroalgae also exhibited high local abundance in other areas, but were absent at REA site TAU-10, located in a predominantly sandy area.

--- SENTENCE 3496 ---
*Halimeda* was the most abundant macroalgae, occurring at 42% of the sampled sites in 2006 (Fig. 5.6.1f).

--- SENTENCE 3497 ---
A dramatic difference in the number of algal genera and their abundance around Ta`u was reported between the 2004 and 2006 survey periods (Fig. 5.6.3a).

--- SENTENCE 3498 ---
It is hypothesized that that the macroalgal community, in particular, may have been scoured by high wave energy generated by tropical cyclone Heta in January 2004, but that the community had recovered by 2006.

--- SENTENCE 3499 ---
Crustose coralline algae were most abundant in the east region, covering up to 50% of the substrate during ASRAMP 2004 (Fig.

--- SENTENCE 3500 ---
Low occurrence and abundance of coralline algal diseases were noted around Ta`u. Ta`u contained only 4.2% of the region-wide total of coralline algae disease cases (21 infections observed), and the cases were distributed over only 30% of the surveyed sites (Figs.

--- SENTENCE 3501 ---
Macroinvertebrate distributions were relatively similar along the forereefs of Ta`u during the 2004 and 2006 surveys (Figs.

--- SENTENCE 3502 ---
Giant clams were present at all but one site, TAU-04, off the north coast of Ta`u (Figs.

--- SENTENCE 3503 ---
In general, giant clams have been more prevalent in the north and west regions and least common on the south side of the island.

--- SENTENCE 3504 ---
No COTS were recorded during any survey.

--- SENTENCE 3505 ---
Sea urchins have been observed at most REA sites around the island during most years of surveying, with the boring urchin *Echinostrephus* sp. being the most common species.

--- SENTENCE 3506 ---
During each of the three ASRAMP cruises, the distribution of sea urchins has been observed to be concentrated on the northwestern corner of the island (Figs.

--- SENTENCE 3507 ---
5.7.1a, 5.7.1b, and 5.7.1d), with concentrations on the northeastern and southwestern corners in some years as well.

--- SENTENCE 3508 ---
Interestingly, the corners of the island have relatively low percentages of coral (Fig. 5.3.2e), but it is not known if there is a link between the coral and urchin distributions.

--- SENTENCE 3509 ---
Sea cucumbers were most prevalent in the west region of the island, but have also been observed at other locations.

--- SENTENCE 3510 ---
Three sea cucumber species were observed around Ta`u (*Holothuria cinerascens*, *Bohadschia argus*, *Holothuria whitmaei*) and were present at all REA sites along the west coast.

--- SENTENCE 3511 ---
Total fish biomass was fairly consistent around the island, and relatively low at 0.7 tons ha-1 (Figs.

--- SENTENCE 3512 ---
5.8.1a, 5.8.1c, and 5.8.1e).

--- SENTENCE 3513 ---
Fish communities were dominated by herbivores and a noticeable presence of small predators (e.g., triggerfish, emperor, and wrasse).

--- SENTENCE 3514 ---
The biomass of large (> 50 cm total length) fish was distributed relatively evenly around the island, considering data from all survey years, and was dominated by parrotfish, snappers, and surgeonfish.

--- SENTENCE 3515 ---
The only clear richness pattern that emerges is a generally lower species count 100 m-2 on the northern side of Ta`u (Figs. 5.8.1b, 5.8.1d, and 5.8.1f).

--- SENTENCE 3516 ---
By way of comparison, at the uninhabited Rose Atoll, large fish biomass was mostly composed of barracuda, jacks, and snappers.

--- SENTENCE 3517 ---

#### <span id="page-308-0"></span>**Chapter 6 Rose Atoll**

# **6.1 Geopolitical Context**

Rose Atoll is an uninhabited, diamond-shaped atoll located at the far eastern end of the American Samoa Archipelago, approximately 300 km east of Tutuila Island.

--- SENTENCE 3526 ---
The barrier reef encloses approximately 6.5 km<sup>2</sup> (~ 1600 acres) of lagoonal habitat, with a 40-m wide channel located in the northern corner of the atoll.

--- SENTENCE 3527 ---
It remains one of the smallest atolls in the world, with Sand Island located in the north and Rose Island located in the east.

--- SENTENCE 3528 ---
These land areas total around 0.06 km2 (~ 15 acres; United States Fish and Wildlife Service).

--- SENTENCE 3529 ---
While Rose Island is vegetated, neither island has any streams, associated watershed areas or notable freshwater sources.

--- SENTENCE 3530 ---
Rose is a National Wildlife Refuge administered by the United States Fish and Wildlife Service within the Pacific Remote Islands National Wildlife Refuge Complex.

#### **6.2 Survey Effort**

A large amount of physical and biological data has been collected around Rose since 2002 as part of the American Samoa Reef Assessment and Monitoring Program (ASRAMP).

--- SENTENCE 3531 ---
* Locations of Rapid Ecological Assessment (REA) and towed-diver surveys around Rose during ASRAMP 2002, 2004, and 2006.

extent and timeframe of these surveys are discussed below.

--- SENTENCE 3534 ---

--- SENTENCE 3535 ---
Benthic habitat mapping data were collected around Rose using acoustic multibeam survey methods, which mapped a total of 269 km2 in and around Rose during ASRAMP 2006.

# <span id="page-311-0"></span>**6.3 Benthic Habitat Mapping and Characterization**

Benthic habitat mapping and characterization around Rose were accomplished using acoustic multibeam sonar between water depths of ~ 1 m and ~ 3000 m. Acoustic multibeam sonar mapping provided bathymetric and acoustic backscatter data in the depth range between ~10 m and 3000 m. Nearshore habitat mapping was conducted using towed-diver benthic surveys between ~ 1 m (lagoon) and 30 m (forereef).

# **6.3.1 Acoustic Mapping and Optical Validation**

Multibeam mapping operations were conducted around Rose in early 2006 by the R/V *Acoustic Habitat Investigator* (*AHI*) and the NOAA Ship *Hi`ialakai* (Fig. 6.3.1a).

--- SENTENCE 3562 ---
Favorable conditions allowed the *AHI* to enter the lagoon through the narrow pass on the NW arm of the island to survey in the interior lagoon area.

--- SENTENCE 3563 ---
No optical data were collected around Rose because of the difficulty of maneuvering vessels close to this extremely steep atoll and limited areas within the depth range of the optical equipment.

--- SENTENCE 3564 ---
Much like Swains Island, Rose is a steeply sloped, conical emergent atoll with rift zones that extend from each corner of the reef down to at least 3000 m. The bathymetry immediately

The north side of the atoll has a small shelf, while the rest is surrounded by steep underwater slopes.

--- SENTENCE 3567 ---
The lagoon contains a scattering of small coral heads and a few large coral outcrops; it reached a maximum recorded depth of 27 m in some places.

# **6.4.1 Hydrographic Data**

#### *2002 Spatial Surveys*

During ASRAMP 2002, 28 shallow-water CTD casts were conducted in the nearshore and lagoonal waters around Rose on February 26 (Figs.

--- SENTENCE 3613 ---
Data from these vertical profiles around the outside of the atoll showed two main water masses: warmer (> 30°C), lower salinity (< 35.3 psu), less dense (< 22 kg m-3) water off the northwest and northeast regions (A–C), and cooler (~ 29.5°C), higher salinity (> 35.3 psu), higher density (> 22 kg m-3) waters off the southwest and southeast regions (C–E) (Fig. 6.4.1b).

--- SENTENCE 3614 ---
The southwest and southeast sides of the atoll showed greater stratification, with warm surface water, a temperate central water column, and cooler bottom (> 20 m) waters.

--- SENTENCE 3615 ---
These data suggest that the southern sides of the atoll may have been more protected from wind and wave-induced mixing, while the northern sides were more exposed to these forces, resulting in vertical mixing (or overturning) of warm surface waters into the main water column.

#### <span id="page-321-0"></span>*2004 Spatial Surveys*

During ASRAMP 2004, 44 evenly spaced, shallow-water CTD casts were conducted in nearshore waters around Rose between February 9 and 11 (Fig. 6.4.1d).

--- SENTENCE 3625 ---
These vertical profiles conducted along the steep forereef slopes around the atoll show significant spatial and vertical structure (Fig.

--- SENTENCE 3626 ---
Near the west point (A) of the northwest region, the water column was well mixed vertically with warm temperatures (> 29.1°C), low beam transmission (< 91%), and moderate salinity (35.4 psu) throughout the column.

--- SENTENCE 3627 ---
Strikingly, the area near the channel and around the north point (B) had cool (~ 28.9°C), low salinity (34.8 psu), and low density (21.9 kg m-3) water in the surface layer (0– ~ 10 m) overlaying a mid-depth water mass with warm (29.1°C) temperatures in depths between 10 and 20 m, and cool (28.9°C), high salinity (35.5 psu) and density (22.4 kg m-3) water in depths between 20 and 35 m).

--- SENTENCE 3628 ---
This complex, highly stratified feature appears to reflect a discharge of fresh surface water from the lagoon out the channel.

--- SENTENCE 3629 ---
The remainder of the northeast forereef (B–C) was well mixed with moderate values for each of the observed water properties.

--- SENTENCE 3630 ---
The southeast region (C–D), on the other hand, was characterized by significant vertical structure, with an interesting plume of cool (28.7°C), high salinity (35.5 psu), and high beam transmission (~ 94%) water near the bottom (20–35 m), particularly near the eastern point (C).

--- SENTENCE 3631 ---
This feature appeared to disperse upward and southward.

#### 6.4.2 Temporal Comparison

--- SENTENCE 3671 ---
—Hydrographic Data

During each of the ASRAMP survey periods in 2002, 2004 and 2006, the nearshore CTD and water quality observations exhibited surprisingly high levels of spatial heterogeneity, given the small area of the atoll and its exposure to the surrounding ocean environment.

--- SENTENCE 3672 ---
Though somewhat small in magnitude, temperature and salinity variations around and within the atoll were notable.

--- SENTENCE 3673 ---
While some of the spatial patterns changed, the actual range of values of most of the water properties did not vary considerably among survey years.

--- SENTENCE 3674 ---
Lagoon salinity and density values were consistently high at a 20-m depth, suggesting that water residence times below the sill depth may be substantial.

#### **6.5.3 Temporal Comparison—Coral and Coral Disease**

Live scleractinian coral cover observed in towed-diver benthic surveys around Rose during the three ASRAMP cruises remained relatively consistent.

--- SENTENCE 3886 ---
Coral cover on the forereef habitats ranged from 20.1% (SE 1.8; 2006) to 29.1% (SE 2.0; 2002; Fig.

--- SENTENCE 3887 ---
Coral cover in the lagoon was markedly lower, ranging from 1.5% (SE 0.5; 2004) to 5.9% (SE 0.9; 2006; Fig. 6.5.3b).

--- SENTENCE 3888 ---
Forereef coral cover data from towed-diver surveys and REA surveys were relatively similar, with island-wide mean differences no greater than ~ 15%.

--- SENTENCE 3889 ---
In contrast, the estimate of REA mean live coral cover in the lagoon was extremely uncertain, as depicted by the high standard error (Fig. 6.5.3b).

--- SENTENCE 3890 ---
Percent cover of live coral from REA surveys was consistently higher than values recorded during the towed-diver benthic surveys (Fig. 6.5.3b).

--- SENTENCE 3891 ---
This difference was probably a result of REA site selection, which targeted hard-bottom substrate and coral pinnacles.

--- SENTENCE 3892 ---

<span id="page-353-0"></span>richness at forereef sites did not vary substantially between 2004 and 2006 (Fig. 6.5.3c), but somewhat higher generic richness was documented at the two lagoon sites in 2006 than in 2004 (Fig. 6.5.3d); site ROS-02 off the southeast corner of Rose exhibited the highest diversity (16-17 genera) and site ROS-07 in the southwest region (the ship grounding site) with the lowest recorded diversity (7-9 genera) in both quantitative survey years.

--- SENTENCE 3912 ---
Interestingly, site ROS-02, which had the highest generic diversity, also had low coral cover, thereby supporting two points stressed throughout this report: (1) different quantitative parameters describing coral communities (percent cover, colony density, diversity) were not necessarily congruent in the magnitude of their values at a given site, and (2) more than a single parameter should be considered in assessing the value or condition of coral communities.

--- SENTENCE 3913 ---
Atoll-wide, mean coral colony densities increased from 4.4 colonies m-2 in 2004 to 6.8 colonies m-2 in 2006 (Figs. 6.5.3e and 6.5.3f).

--- SENTENCE 3914 ---
Even when site ROS-22, which was not resurveyed in 2006, was removed from the analysis, there was a substantial difference noted between mean coral density at Rose between 2004 and 2006.

--- SENTENCE 3915 ---
As with the apparent parallel increase in coral density at Ofu/Olosega and at Ta`u from 2004 to 2006, it is difficult to know if this potential change, which could result from new recruits to the population or fragmentation/fissioning of existing colonies, is "real" or an artifact of interobserver error.

--- SENTENCE 3916 ---
In this regard, it is interesting to note that site ROS-03 was observed to have among the lowest coral densities in 2004 (2.9 colonies m-2) but the highest coral density in 2006 (10.4 colonies m-2).

--- SENTENCE 3917 ---
During ASRAMP 2006, two coral biologists conducted population parameter surveys.

--- SENTENCE 3918 ---
One biologist enumerated all colonies > 5 cm maximum diameter, while the second biologist closely inspected the benthos for very small (< 5 cm) colonies.

--- SENTENCE 3919 ---
While this experimental alteration of survey protocols, which was undertaken only at site ROS-03, may result in more accurate data, it appeared to have biased temporal comparisons as a result of the increased small colony search effort.

--- SENTENCE 3920 ---
This provided another useful lesson for stabilizing personnel allocations and method protocols in 2008 so that improved comparisons could be made in future surveys.

--- SENTENCE 3921 ---
The lack of large (> 80 cm) colonies at Rose in 2004 and 2006 suggests that most large corals at the shallow depths died after the 1994 bleaching event, and that coral recovery remains ongoing (Figs. 6.5.3g and 6.5.3h).

--- SENTENCE 3922 ---
The proportion of corals in medium (20–40 cm) and medium-large (40–80 cm) size classes was reduced in 2006 compared to 2004.

--- SENTENCE 3923 ---
Overall, 48% of corals belonged to these size classes (i.e., 20–80 cm) in 2004, compared to 31% in 2006.

--- SENTENCE 3924 ---
The correspondingly higher proportion of corals in smaller size classes in 2006 (i.e. 0–20 cm) was consistent with the calculated higher density values.

--- SENTENCE 3925 ---
Hurricanes Olaf and Percy in early 2005, which may have moved the anchored 1200-lb CREWS buoy inside the protected lagoon, could potentially explain the smaller corals observed in 2006.

--- SENTENCE 3926 ---
These tropical cyclones may have caused considerable damage to the shallower reefs, including fragmentation of corals, resulting in increased densities and a shift to smaller size classes.

#### **6.6 Algae**

#### **6.6.1 Algal Surveys**

It is important to note when considering these results that turf algae, crustose coralline red

<span id="page-354-0"></span>algae, branched non-geniculate coralline red algae, and cyanophytes (blue-green algae) all need to be analyzed microscopically for proper taxonomic identification and therefore, must be lumped into functional group categories in the field.

--- SENTENCE 3927 ---
Of these functional groups, turf algae are the most diverse with the possibility of up to 100 species occurring in a 10 cm2 area.

--- SENTENCE 3928 ---
As well, macroalgae are large, fleshy, sometimes calcified entities that may be identifiable to genus or species in the field, but often require microscopic analysis to confirm taxonomic identities.

--- SENTENCE 3929 ---
# *2002 Spatial Surveys*

A total of 18 towed-diver benthic surveys were conducted around Rose during ASRAMP 2002.

--- SENTENCE 3930 ---
Fleshy macroalgae and crustose coralline red algae covered, on average, 58.1% of the forereef and 10.3% of the backreef and lagoon substrate.

--- SENTENCE 3931 ---
On the forereef habitats, mean fleshy macroalgal cover was 19.0% (SE 0.9) and mean crustose coralline algal cover was 39.1% (SE 1.5) of the benthic substrate (Fig.

--- SENTENCE 3932 ---
On the backreef and lagoon habitats, mean fleshy macroalgal cover was 10.2% (SE 1.6), and mean crustose coralline algal cover was 10.2% (SE 0.8; Fig.

--- SENTENCE 3933 ---
Highest percent cover of fleshy macroalgae was observed along the northwest, southwest, and southeast forereef slopes of the atoll.

--- SENTENCE 3934 ---
The highest percent cover of crustose coralline algae was observed near the westernmost, easternmost, and southernmost points of the atoll, all likely areas of moderate-to-high wave energy and current flow.

--- SENTENCE 3935 ---
Lowest coralline algal cover was observed in the lagoon.

--- SENTENCE 4055 ---
